incidente.resumo: During a name server IP address rollout, a Puppet manifest bug restarted only the authoritative name server, so the caching server queried an IP no longer serving DNS. A DNS deploy during the investigation, built from a provisioning API call that needed DNS, removed many records (NXDOMAIN), and fileservers hit memory exhaustion. Reloading the name servers, manually restoring records and removing and repairing fileservers restored service: 42 minutes of downtime plus 1 hour 35 minutes for some repositories.
servicos_afetados: repositories on a subset of fileservers

descricao.texto: Problems began nearly immediately after the deploy to the second name server: certain DNS queries were observed to be timing out.
trechos: We proceeded to deploy to the second name server at 13:29 PM PST, and again performed the same verification.
However, problems began manifesting nearly immediately.
We began to observe that certain DNS queries were timing out.

gatilho.texto: A rollout of firewall, router and DNS server configuration changes updating the IP addresses the name servers used began at 13:20 PST on the first DNS server and was deployed to the second name server at 13:29 PST, after which problems began nearly immediately.
trechos: In order to roll out these changes, we had prepared changes to our firewall and router configuration to update the IP addresses our name servers used to send queries and receive responses.
In addition, we prepared similar changes to our DNS server configuration to allow them to use these new IP addresses.
Our rollout began on the afternoon of the 8th at 13:20 PM PST.
We proceeded to deploy to the second name server at 13:29 PM PST, and again performed the same verification.
However, problems began manifesting nearly immediately.

descricao.texto: Both the caching and authoritative name servers received the new configuration, but due to a bug in the Puppet manifests only the authoritative name server was restarted; the caching name server kept requesting authoritative DNS records from an IP that no longer served DNS, creating the initial connection timeouts.
trechos: Both name servers received the appropriate configuration changes, but only the authoritative name server was restarted due to a bug in our Puppet manifests.
As a result, our caching name server was requesting authoritative DNS records from an IP that was no longer serving DNS.
This bug created the initial connection timeouts we observed, and began a cascade of events.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: A DNS system deployment triggered during the investigation built the zone file from an API call to the internal provisioning system that itself requires functioning DNS, and its output was not adequately sanity-checked; the deployment removed a significant amount of records, causing NXDOMAIN results.
trechos: Further investigation found that our DNS zone files had become corrupted due to a circular dependency between our internal provisioning service and DNS.

During the investigation of the first phase of this incident, we triggered a deployment of our DNS system, which performs an API call against our internal provisioning system and uses the result of this call to construct a zone file.
However, this query requires a functioning DNS infrastructure to complete successfully.
Further, the output from this API call verification was not adequately checked for sanity before being converted into a zone file.
As a result, this deployment removed a significant amount of records from our name servers, causing the `NXDOMAIN` results we observed.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: After many servers recovered once DNS responded, github.com performance had not returned to normal and error rates were far higher than normal; investigation found a subset of fileservers refusing connections due to memory exhaustion, exacerbated by the spawning of a significant number of processes during the DNS outage.
trechos: Many of our servers recovered gracefully once DNS service began responding appropriately.
However, we quickly noted that github.com performance had not returned to normal, and our error rates were far higher than normal.

Further investigation found that a subset of our fileservers were actively refusing connections due to what we found out later was memory exhaustion, exacerbated by the spawning of a significant number of processes on during the DNS outage.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The failing fileservers created back pressure in the routing layer that prevented connections to healthy fileservers, and protective measures meant to automatically remove such servers from service did not fire as designed.
trechos: The failing fileservers began creating a back pressure in our routing layer that prevented connections to healthy fileservers.

During the failure when filesevers became so exhausted that the routing layer failed due to back pressure, we should have seen several protective measures kick in to automatically remove these servers from service.
These mechanisms did not fire off as designed, and need to be revisited.

descricao.texto: Changes to the firewall, router and DNS server configuration that updated the IP addresses the name servers used to send queries and receive responses.
trechos: In order to roll out these changes, we had prepared changes to our firewall and router configuration to update the IP addresses our name servers used to send queries and receive responses.
In addition, we prepared similar changes to our DNS server configuration to allow them to use these new IP addresses.

passos.texto: The caching and authoritative name servers were reloaded at 13:49 PST, resolving the DNS query timeouts.
trechos: Our caching and authoritative name servers were reloaded at 13:49 PST, resolving DNS query timeouts.

passos.texto: The missing DNS records were restored by performing the provisioning API call manually, validating the output, and updating the affected zones.
trechos: The missing DNS records were restored by performing the API call manually, validating the output, and updating the affected zones.

passos.texto: The team manually removed all misbehaving fileservers from the routing layer, restoring service for the fileservers that had survived the spike in processes and memory.
trechos: Our team began manually removing all misbehaving fileservers from the routing layer, restoring services for the fileservers that had survived the spike in processes and memory during the DNS event.

passos.texto: On disabled fileservers, either an engineer logged in and forcefully killed hung processes, or the HA daemon had used STONITH on the active node and brought up the secondary node; DRBD block devices were then checked for replication inconsistencies, and full service was restored for all customers by 15:47 PST.
trechos: Collectively, we found one of two scenarios existed to be repaired: either the node had calmed down ‘enough’ as a result of DNS service restoration to allow one of our engineers to log into the box and start forcefully killing hung processes to restore service, or the node had become so exhausted that our HA daemon kicked in to STONITH the active node and bring up our secondary node.
In both of these situations, our team went in and performed checks against our low-level DRBD block devices to ensure there were no inconsistencies or errors in data replication.
Full service was restored for all of our customers by 15:47 PM PST.

acoes.texto: Under investigation: further decoupling of the internal and external DNS infrastructure so changes can happen independently.
trechos: We are investigating further decoupling of our internal and external DNS infrastructure.

While the pattern of forwarding requests to an upstream DNS server is not uncommon, the tight dependency that exists between our internal name servers and our external name servers needs to be broken up to allow changes to happen independently of each other.

acoes.texto: In progress: reviewing configuration management code for other service restart bugs, including reviewing critical code for tests using rspec-puppet and looking at integration tests for service management.
trechos: We are reviewing our configuration management code for other service restart bugs.
We will be reviewing critical code for appropriate tests using `rspec-puppet`, as well as looking at integration tests to ensure that service management behaves as intended.

acoes.texto: Already done: the deployment procedure was updated to verify the results returned from the provisioning API call before removing a large number of records; the cyclic dependency between the provisioning system and DNS resolvers is under review.
trechos: We are reviewing the cyclic dependency between our internal provisioning system and our DNS resolvers, and have already updated the deployment procedure to verify the results returned from the API call before removing a large number of records.

acoes.texto: In progress: reviewing and testing the safety release valves in the fileserver management systems and routing layers, which did not fire as designed.
trechos: We are reviewing and testing all of the designed safety release valves in our fileserver management systems and routing layers.
These mechanisms did not fire off as designed, and need to be revisited.

acoes.texto: In progress: implementing process accounting controls to limit resources consumed by application processes, testing Linux cgroups to isolate application processes from administrative system functionality.
trechos: We are implementing process accounting controls to appropriately limit the resources consumed by our application processes.
Specifically, we are testing Linux `cgroups` to further isolate application processes from administrative system functionality.

acoes.texto: In progress: reviewing code deployed to the fileservers for tight dependencies on DNS.
trechos: We are reviewing the code deployed to our fileservers to analyze for tight dependencies to DNS.

As a result of this outage, our customers experienced 42 minutes of downtime of services along with an additional 1 hour and 35 minutes of downtime within a subset of repositories as we worked to restore full service.

observacoes: The text gives the date as 'Wednesday, January 8th' without a year, so data_incidente is null. Duration is the stated 42 minutes of downtime plus the additional 1 hour 35 minutes for a subset of repositories (137 minutes); the times in the text (second name server deploy at 13:29 PST, full service at 15:47 PST) give 138 minutes.
